#### 1. muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy (congenital with impaired intellectual development), type B, 15  —  Tier 1 — Definitive / Highly Plausible  (fitness 0.742)
**Link type:** shared causal gene (HGNC:3007)

**Proposed mechanism:** DPM3 (HGNC:3007) —DISRUPTS→ Dolichol pathway of GPI anchor synthesis; Dolichol pathway of GPI anchor synthesis —DECREASES→ Glycoprotein glycosylation; Glycoprotein glycosylation —DECREASES→ Dystroglycan function; Dystroglycan function —LEADS_TO→ Impaired neurological development (HP:0011344); Dystroglycan function —LEADS_TO→ Muscle development abnormalities (HP:0003198). Loss-of-function mutations in DPM3 disrupt the dolichol pathway, leading to impaired glycoprotein glycosylation. This downstream effect impacts dystroglycan function, manifesting as both neurological and muscle development abnormalities, thus linking the two diseases.

**How to falsify it:** Identification of a pathogenic variant in DPM3 with a significantly high allele frequency (e.g., >1% in gnomAD) in the general population would falsify its role as a causal gene for these rare diseases. _(variant: HGNC:3007)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared genetic basis in DPM3 provides a common therapeutic target for both MONDO:0013049 and muscular dystrophy-dystroglycanopathy type B15, potentially enabling the development of gene- or pathway-targeted therapies that could benefit patients with either condition.

Mutations in DPM1 and DPM3 disrupt the dolichol phosphate pathway, leading to a spectrum of developmental and neurological phenotypes common to both diseases.

**How to falsify it:** Demonstration that mutations in DPM1 or DPM3 do not impair the dolichol phosphate pathway's function in cellular models, or identification of a significant pathogenic variant in these genes with a frequency >1% in gnomAD. _(variant: Exome Variant Frequency > 0.01)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared mechanism in the dolichol phosphate pathway provides a common therapeutic target for both congenital disorder of glycosylation type 1E and the related disorder caused by DPM3 mutations. Interventions aimed at restoring or compensating for defective N-glycosylation could benefit patients with either condition.

#### 3. juvenile-onset diabetes mellitus-central and peripheral neurodegeneration syndrome  —  Tier 3 — Moderate / Emerging  (fitness 0.448)
**Link type:** shared pathway (Reactome:R-HSA-9918432)

**Proposed mechanism:** DPM3 (HGNC:2779) —DISRUPTS→ dolichol-linked oligosaccharide synthesis (GO:0006499); dolichol-linked oligosaccharide synthesis (GO:0006499) —LEADS_TO→ ER protein folding (GO:0006457); dolichol-linked oligosaccharide synthesis (GO:0006499) —LEADS_TO→ glycoprotein processing (GO:0006486); ER protein folding (GO:0006457) —LEADS_TO→ Intellectual disability (HP:0001249); glycoprotein processing (GO:0006486) —LEADS_TO→ Diabetes mellitus (HP:0000820); DNAJC3 (HGNC:17974) —DISRUPTS→ ER protein folding (GO:0006457); DNAJC3 (HGNC:17974) —DISRUPTS→ glycoprotein processing (GO:0006486); ER protein folding (GO:0006457) —LEADS_TO→ Neurodegeneration (HP:0000715). Mutations in DPM3 impair dolichol-linked oligosaccharide synthesis, which is upstream of ER protein folding and glycoprotein processing. Similarly, mutations in DNAJC3, a J-domain protein co-chaperone, directly impair ER protein folding and glycoprotein processing. Both pathways converge on general cellular homeostasis in the ER, leading to downstream neurodegeneration and metabolic dysfunction (diabetes).

**How to falsify it:** Demonstration that DPM3 and DNAJC3 do not converge on common downstream pathways related to ER protein folding and glycoprotein processing, or that mutations in one gene do not affect the cellular processes impacted by mutations in the other. _(variant: Presence of common variants (AF > 0.01) in gnomAD that are predicted to be pathogenic in either DPM3 or DNAJC3, suggesting these are not strictly rare disease genes.)_

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared role of ER protein folding and glycoprotein processing dysfunction in these distinct rare diseases could reveal common therapeutic targets for neurodegenerative and metabolic conditions.

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared role of the dolichol phosphate pathway in these distinct rare diseases could pave the way for targeted therapies aimed at restoring protein glycosylation, potentially ameliorating neurological and muscular symptoms in both conditions.
